items.stem: Which statement describes the particles in a solid?
options: They are close together but move randomly past one another.
They are far apart and move randomly at high speed.
They are closely packed in a regular arrangement and move freely past one another.
They are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.
items.answer: They are closely packed in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.
items.markingKey: Solid: regular lattice, particles touching, vibrate only.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why a solid has a fixed shape.
items.answer: The particles are held in fixed positions in a regular lattice by strong forces of attraction; they can only vibrate and cannot move past one another.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strong forces / fixed positions; 1 mark: particles only vibrate, cannot move past each other [2]

items.stem: Explain, using the kinetic particle model, why liquids cannot be compressed but gases can.
items.answer: Liquid particles are already touching with almost no space between them; gas particles are far apart with large spaces, so they can be pushed closer together.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: liquid particles close together / touching; 1 mark: gas particles far apart, spaces can be reduced [2]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. propanone: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 56 °C; nitrogen: m.p. −210 °C, b.p. −196 °C; ammonia: m.p. −78 °C, b.p. −33 °C; potassium bromide: m.p. 734 °C, b.p. 1435 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at 1000 °C.
items.answer: propanone: gas; nitrogen: gas; ammonia: gas; potassium bromide: liquid
items.markingKey: propanone: gas; nitrogen: gas; ammonia: gas; potassium bromide: liquid. Solid if 1000 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: Data for 5 substances are shown. magnesium: m.p. 650 °C, b.p. 1090 °C; hexane: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 69 °C; mercury: m.p. −39 °C, b.p. 357 °C; potassium bromide: m.p. 734 °C, b.p. 1435 °C; oxygen: m.p. −218 °C, b.p. −183 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at −50 °C.
items.answer: magnesium: solid; hexane: liquid; mercury: solid; potassium bromide: solid; oxygen: gas
items.markingKey: magnesium: solid; hexane: liquid; mercury: solid; potassium bromide: solid; oxygen: gas. Solid if −50 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [5]

items.stem: Data for 5 substances are shown. sulfur: m.p. 115 °C, b.p. 445 °C; copper: m.p. 1085 °C, b.p. 2562 °C; chlorine: m.p. −101 °C, b.p. −34 °C; nitrogen: m.p. −210 °C, b.p. −196 °C; hexane: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 69 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at 100 °C. State the range of temperature over which nitrogen is a liquid and describe the movement of its particles in that range.
items.answer: sulfur: solid; copper: solid; chlorine: gas; nitrogen: gas; hexane: gas. Nitrogen is a liquid from −210 °C to −196 °C; particles move randomly, sliding past one another.
items.markingKey: sulfur: solid; copper: solid; chlorine: gas; nitrogen: gas; hexane: gas. Nitrogen is a liquid from −210 °C to −196 °C; particles move randomly, sliding past one another.. 1 mark per correct state [5]; range [1]; movement [1]

items.stem: Amara researches sodium chloride, which has a melting point of 801 °C and a boiling point of 1413 °C. (a) State the physical state of sodium chloride at 869 °C and at 1267 °C. (b) Predict whether the forces of attraction between the particles of this substance are strong or weak. Explain your answer using the data.
items.answer: (a) liquid at 869 °C; liquid at 1267 °C (b) Strong: the melting and boiling points are high, so much energy is needed to overcome the forces.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: strong/weak; 1 mark: linked to m.p./b.p. data [2]

items.stem: In a chemistry club, a sealed sample of substance Y (m.p. 207 °C, b.p. 490 °C) is studied at different temperatures. (a) Explain, in terms of particles, why substance Y at 355 °C takes the shape of its container but keeps a fixed volume. (b) Suggest a temperature at which substance Y would be a liquid. (c) Predict whether the forces of attraction between the particles of this substance are strong or weak. Explain your answer using the data.
items.answer: (a) Particles are close together so the volume is fixed, but they move past one another so the shape changes. (b) any temperature between 207 °C and 490 °C, e.g. 348 °C (c) Strong: the melting and boiling points are high, so much energy is needed to overcome the forces.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) between m.p. and b.p. [1] (c) 1 mark: strong/weak; 1 mark: linked to m.p./b.p. data [2]

items.stem: Which property is shared by liquids and gases but not by solids?
options: They can flow and take the shape of their container.
items.answer: They can flow and take the shape of their container.
items.markingKey: Particles in liquids and gases can move past one another, so both flow.

items.stem: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
items.answer: liquid
items.markingKey: Liquid particles are close together (fixed volume) but can move past each other (no fixed shape).

items.stem: Explain why a gas spreads out to fill any container it is put in.
items.answer: Gas particles move rapidly and randomly in all directions and the forces between them are negligible, so they spread into all the available space.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: rapid random movement; 1 mark: negligible attractive forces [2]

items.stem: A student says, "The particles in a solid do not move." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions; they have kinetic energy but cannot move from place to place.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles vibrate; 1 mark: about fixed positions / do not change position [2]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. iron: m.p. 1538 °C, b.p. 2862 °C; hexane: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 69 °C; mercury: m.p. −39 °C, b.p. 357 °C; iodine: m.p. 114 °C, b.p. 184 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at 500 °C.
items.answer: iron: solid; hexane: gas; mercury: gas; iodine: gas
items.markingKey: iron: solid; hexane: gas; mercury: gas; iodine: gas. Solid if 500 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. ethanol: m.p. −114 °C, b.p. 78 °C; chlorine: m.p. −101 °C, b.p. −34 °C; potassium bromide: m.p. 734 °C, b.p. 1435 °C; copper: m.p. 1085 °C, b.p. 2562 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at 0 °C.
items.answer: ethanol: liquid; chlorine: gas; potassium bromide: solid; copper: solid
items.markingKey: ethanol: liquid; chlorine: gas; potassium bromide: solid; copper: solid. Solid if 0 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: A data book in Mexico City gives the melting point of substance A as 781 °C and its boiling point as 983 °C. (a) Explain, in terms of particles, why substance A at 293 °C has a fixed shape. (b) Suggest a temperature at which substance A would be a liquid. (c) Predict whether the forces of attraction between the particles of this substance are strong or weak. Explain your answer using the data.
items.answer: (a) Strong forces hold particles in fixed positions; they only vibrate. (b) any temperature between 781 °C and 983 °C, e.g. 882 °C (c) Strong: the melting and boiling points are high, so much energy is needed to overcome the forces.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) between m.p. and b.p. [1] (c) 1 mark: strong/weak; 1 mark: linked to m.p./b.p. data [2]

items.stem: Noah researches argon, which has a melting point of −189 °C and a boiling point of −186 °C. (a) Explain, in terms of particles, why argon at −119 °C can be compressed. (b) Suggest a temperature at which argon would be a liquid.
items.answer: (a) Particles are far apart with large spaces between them that can be reduced. (b) any temperature between −189 °C and −186 °C, e.g. −188 °C
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) between m.p. and b.p. [1]

items.stem: Ethan researches substance C, which has a melting point of −122 °C and a boiling point of 404 °C. (a) State the physical state of substance C at 215 °C and at 438 °C. (b) Describe the arrangement and movement of the particles at 438 °C. (c) Suggest a temperature at which substance C would be a liquid.
items.answer: (a) liquid at 215 °C; gas at 438 °C (b) far apart and randomly arranged; move rapidly and randomly in all directions (c) any temperature between −122 °C and 404 °C, e.g. 141 °C
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark arrangement; 1 mark movement [2] (c) between m.p. and b.p. [1]

items.stem: What is the name of the change of state from gas to liquid?
items.answer: condensation
items.markingKey: Gas → liquid is condensation; energy is released.

items.stem: Explain the difference between boiling and evaporation.
items.answer: Boiling happens at a fixed temperature (the boiling point) throughout the liquid, with bubbles forming; evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature below the boiling point.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: boiling at b.p. throughout liquid; 1 mark: evaporation at surface, below b.p. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the temperature stays constant while a pure solid is melting, even though it is still being heated.
items.answer: The energy supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles rather than to increase their kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: energy overcomes attractive forces; 1 mark: not increasing kinetic energy / temperature [2]

items.stem: Isla heats a sample of paraffin wax until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 76 °C, 1 min: 71 °C, 2 min: 66 °C, 3 min: 61 °C, 4 min: 56 °C, 5 min: 56 °C, 6 min: 56 °C, 7 min: 56 °C, 8 min: 56 °C, 9 min: 50 °C, 10 min: 44 °C, 11 min: 38 °C. Use the results to state the freezing point of the sample and the physical state(s) present at 5 min.
items.answer: 56 °C; liquid and solid together
items.markingKey: 1 mark: freezing point; 1 mark: solid and liquid [2]

items.stem: Jonas heats a sample of paraffin wax until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 91 °C, 1 min: 86 °C, 2 min: 81 °C, 3 min: 76 °C, 4 min: 71 °C, 5 min: 66 °C, 6 min: 61 °C, 7 min: 56 °C, 8 min: 56 °C, 9 min: 56 °C, 10 min: 56 °C, 11 min: 56 °C, 12 min: 52 °C, 13 min: 48 °C, 14 min: 44 °C. (a) State the physical state(s) present at 0 min and at 8 min. (b) Calculate how long the substance took to freeze completely, according to these readings.
items.answer: (a) liquid; liquid and solid (b) about 4 min
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 11 − 7 = 4 min [1]

items.stem: Diego heats a solid sample of hexane at a steady rate from −135 °C until it has all turned to gas at 89 °C. (a) Explain why the flat section for boiling is usually longer than the one for melting. (b) Describe the changes in the arrangement and movement of particles as the hexane melts.
items.answer: (a) More energy is needed to separate particles completely (overcome nearly all attractive forces) when boiling than to let them move past each other when melting. (b) Particles go from a regular arrangement vibrating about fixed points to a random arrangement sliding past one another.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: more energy for boiling; 1 mark: forces overcome completely / particles separated [2] (b) 1 mark arrangement; 1 mark movement [2]

items.stem: Which substance sublimes when it is warmed at atmospheric pressure?
items.answer: solid carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: Dry ice (solid CO₂) changes directly from solid to gas.

items.stem: Explain why sweating cools the body.
items.answer: Water in sweat evaporates; the particles that escape have the most energy, so the average kinetic energy (temperature) of what remains falls, taking energy from the skin.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: evaporation needs energy / most energetic particles escape; 1 mark: energy taken from skin [2]

items.stem: Explain why a puddle dries faster on a warm, windy day than on a cold, still day.
items.answer: Higher temperature gives more particles enough energy to escape from the surface; wind removes vapour so particles do not return to the liquid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: temperature effect; 1 mark: wind effect [2]

items.stem: A sample of argon is heated steadily from −219 °C to −156 °C and a heating curve is plotted. Which state(s) are present during the first rising section of the curve? Give the temperature of the first flat section and explain why the temperature is constant there.
items.answer: solid; flat sections at −189 °C (melting) and −186 °C (boiling); energy supplied overcomes attractive forces instead of raising kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: state(s); 1 mark: correct temperature; 1 mark: energy used to overcome forces [3]

items.stem: A sample of iron is heated steadily from 1508 °C to 2892 °C and a heating curve is plotted. Which state(s) are present during the first rising section of the curve? Give the temperature of the second flat section and explain why the temperature is constant there.
items.answer: solid; flat sections at 1538 °C (melting) and 2862 °C (boiling); energy supplied overcomes attractive forces instead of raising kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: state(s); 1 mark: correct temperature; 1 mark: energy used to overcome forces [3]

items.stem: Sofia heats a solid sample of chlorine at a steady rate from −141 °C until it has all turned to gas at −14 °C. (a) Explain why the flat section for boiling is usually longer than the one for melting. (b) Describe the changes in the arrangement and movement of particles as the chlorine melts.
items.answer: (a) More energy is needed to separate particles completely (overcome nearly all attractive forces) when boiling than to let them move past each other when melting. (b) Particles go from a regular arrangement vibrating about fixed points to a random arrangement sliding past one another.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: more energy for boiling; 1 mark: forces overcome completely / particles separated [2] (b) 1 mark arrangement; 1 mark movement [2]

items.stem: Hana heats a solid sample of magnesium at a steady rate from 610 °C until it has all turned to gas at 1110 °C. (a) Describe the shape of the heating curve, naming the processes at each flat section. (b) A second student finds that their sample melts between 644 °C and 648 °C. Suggest what this shows about their sample.
items.answer: (a) rises (solid warms), flat at 650 °C (melting), rises (liquid warms), flat at 1090 °C (boiling), rises (gas warms) (b) It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: two flat sections; 1 mark: temperatures; 1 mark: named melting and boiling [3] (b) 1 mark: impure; 1 mark: lower / over a range [2]

items.stem: A fixed mass of gas is heated at constant pressure. What happens to its volume?
items.answer: It increases.
items.markingKey: Particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, pushing them out.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why the volume of a gas increases when it is heated at constant pressure.
items.answer: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster; they hit the walls harder and more often, so the gas pushes outwards and expands until the pressure inside equals the pressure outside.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles move faster / more kinetic energy; 1 mark: more frequent / harder collisions with walls; 1 mark: gas expands [3]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why the volume of a gas decreases when the pressure on it is increased at constant temperature.
items.answer: The particles are far apart, so they can be pushed closer together into a smaller space; the same particles then collide with the walls more often, matching the higher external pressure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles far apart can be pushed closer; 1 mark: more frequent collisions per unit area [2]

items.stem: Leila traps carbon dioxide in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 0 °C: 60.0 cm³, 25 °C: 65.5 cm³, 50 °C: 71.0 cm³, 75 °C: ? cm³, 100 °C: 82.0 cm³. Describe the relationship between temperature and volume shown by the data.
items.answer: As the temperature increases the volume increases (by equal amounts for equal temperature rises).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume increases with temperature; 1 mark: steady / linear [2]

items.stem: Nadia traps air in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 0 °C: 20.0 cm³, 10 °C: 20.7 cm³, 20 °C: 21.5 cm³, 30 °C: ? cm³, 40 °C: 22.9 cm³. (a) State one variable that must be kept constant and explain why. (b) Suggest why the syringe plunger must move freely.
items.answer: (a) The pressure (or the amount/mass of gas, e.g. no leaks), because it also affects the volume. (b) So that the pressure inside stays equal to atmospheric pressure (constant pressure).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: variable; 1 mark: reason [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Tomás investigates how the volume of argon changes. A sample is sealed in a gas syringe and placed in water baths at different temperatures, and then the plunger is pushed in at constant temperature. (a) Describe and explain what happens to the volume when the pressure is increased at constant temperature. (b) Explain what happens when a sealed syringe of air is placed in a beaker of hot water.
items.answer: (a) Volume decreases: particles are far apart and are pushed closer together. (b) The volume increases because the gas is heated; particles move faster.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: particles pushed closer / spaces reduced [2] (b) 1 mark: prediction; 1 mark: particle reason [2]

items.stem: Explain why car tyre pressures should be checked when the tyres are cold.
items.answer: After driving the gas is warmer, its particles move faster and hit the tyre walls more often and harder, so the pressure reading is higher than the true cold value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: temperature raises pressure; 1 mark: particle explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why an aerosol can must not be heated, even when it seems to be empty.
items.answer: There is still gas inside; heating makes its particles move faster and collide with the walls more often and harder, so the pressure rises and the can may explode.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: pressure increases; 1 mark: particles faster / more collisions [2]

items.stem: A student says, "When a gas is cooled, its particles shrink and so the volume goes down." Explain the error.
items.answer: The particles do not change size; they move more slowly, collide with the walls less often and less hard, so the gas contracts at constant pressure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles stay same size; 1 mark: slower / fewer collisions [2]

items.stem: A fixed mass of oxygen is kept at constant temperature while the pressure on it is changed. Results: 100 kPa: 96.0 cm³, 150 kPa: 64.0 cm³, 200 kPa: 48.0 cm³, 300 kPa: 32.0 cm³, 400 kPa: 24.0 cm³. Describe the relationship between pressure and volume shown, and predict the volume at 800 kPa.
items.answer: As pressure increases the volume decreases; doubling the pressure halves the volume (pressure × volume is constant). At 800 kPa the volume would be 12.0 cm³.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume decreases as pressure increases; 1 mark: inverse (doubling P halves V); 1 mark: prediction 12.0 cm³ [3]

items.stem: A fixed mass of helium is kept at constant temperature while the pressure on it is changed. Results: 100 kPa: 60.0 cm³, 125 kPa: 48.0 cm³, 150 kPa: 40.0 cm³, 200 kPa: 30.0 cm³, 250 kPa: 24.0 cm³. Describe the relationship between pressure and volume shown, and predict the volume at 500 kPa.
items.answer: As pressure increases the volume decreases; doubling the pressure halves the volume (pressure × volume is constant). At 500 kPa the volume would be 12.0 cm³.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume decreases as pressure increases; 1 mark: inverse (doubling P halves V); 1 mark: prediction 12.0 cm³ [3]

items.stem: A company in Singapore stores oxygen in cylinders and balloons for use at events. Engineers study how the gas behaves when it is heated, cooled and compressed. (a) Describe and explain what happens to the volume of the gas when it is heated at constant pressure. (b) Suggest why gases are stored under high pressure in cylinders.
items.answer: (a) Volume increases: particles gain kinetic energy, move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, pushing them out. (b) A large amount (mass) of gas can be stored in a small volume because the particles can be pushed close together.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: increases; 1 mark: faster particles; 1 mark: collisions with walls [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Amara investigates how the volume of helium changes. A sample is sealed in a gas syringe and placed in water baths at different temperatures, and then the plunger is pushed in at constant temperature. (a) Describe and explain what happens to the volume of the gas when it is heated at constant pressure. (b) Explain why a sealed rigid cylinder of gas could burst if it is left in a fire. (c) Suggest why gases are stored under high pressure in cylinders.
items.answer: (a) Volume increases: particles gain kinetic energy, move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, pushing them out. (b) The volume cannot increase, so as particles move faster and collide with the walls more often and harder the pressure rises until the cylinder fails. (c) A large amount (mass) of gas can be stored in a small volume because the particles can be pushed close together.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: increases; 1 mark: faster particles; 1 mark: collisions with walls [3] (b) 1 mark: pressure rises at fixed volume; 1 mark: particle explanation [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is meant by diffusion?
options: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration as a result of their random motion
The dissolving of a solid in a liquid
The movement of particles only when a liquid is stirred
The movement of particles from low to high concentration
items.answer: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration as a result of their random motion
items.markingKey: Diffusion: random motion causes net spreading from high to low concentration.

items.stem: Explain why the smell of perfume spreads across a room even when there is no draught.
items.answer: Perfume particles evaporate and move randomly, colliding with air particles; there is a net movement from where the concentration is high to where it is low.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: random movement; 1 mark: high to low concentration [2]

items.stem: Explain why diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids.
items.answer: Gas particles move much faster and are far apart, so they collide less often with other particles; liquid particles are close together and move more slowly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: gas particles faster; 1 mark: fewer collisions / more space [2]

items.stem: Nadia places cotton wool soaked in concentrated aqueous ammonia at one end of a 120 cm glass tube and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrobromic acid at the other end, then seals both ends. After a few minutes a white ring of ammonium bromide forms inside the tube. Calculate the relative molecular masses of ammonia and hydrogen bromide.
items.answer: NH₃ = 17; HBr = 81
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Ana places cotton wool soaked in concentrated aqueous ammonia at one end of a 80 cm glass tube and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrobromic acid at the other end, then seals both ends. After a few minutes a white ring of ammonium bromide forms inside the tube. (a) Explain why the tube is sealed at both ends. (b) The experiment is repeated with a 160 cm tube. Predict the effect on the time taken and on the relative position of the ring.
items.answer: (a) To stop the gases escaping (and to stop air currents/draughts affecting the movement). (b) Takes longer (further to travel); the ring still forms nearer the hydrogen bromide end at the same fraction of the length.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark: longer; 1 mark: same relative position [2]

items.stem: Elena drops a crystal of a food dye into a beaker of still water at 10 °C and times how long it takes for the red colour to spread evenly: 600 s. The experiment is repeated with water at 30 °C: 420 s. (a) State two variables that should be kept the same in both experiments. (b) Calculate the percentage decrease in the time taken.
items.answer: (a) size/mass of crystal; volume of water (also same beaker, no stirring) (b) 30.0%

items.stem: Which gas diffuses fastest at the same temperature?
items.answer: hydrogen
items.markingKey: Lowest Mr (2) → fastest diffusion.

items.stem: Explain why ammonia diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride.
items.answer: Ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17) than hydrogen chloride (36.5), so at the same temperature its molecules move faster.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr comparison; 1 mark: lighter molecules move faster [2]

items.stem: Explain why a coloured dye spreads more quickly through hot water than through cold water.
items.answer: In hot water the particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so they spread out more quickly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more kinetic energy; 1 mark: faster movement / faster diffusion [2]

items.stem: Samples of carbon monoxide, CO, and hydrogen bromide, HBr, are released at the same time and temperature. Which statement is correct? (Ar: Br = 80, C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
options: Hydrogen bromide diffuses faster because it has a lower Mr.
Both diffuse at the same rate because they are both gases.
Carbon monoxide diffuses faster because it has a lower Mr.
Carbon monoxide diffuses faster because its molecules are larger.
items.answer: Carbon monoxide diffuses faster because it has a lower Mr.
items.markingKey: Mr(CO) = 28, Mr(HBr) = 81: lower Mr → faster.

items.stem: Isla, a student in Manila, compares the rates of diffusion of bromine, Br₂, and nitrogen dioxide, NO₂, at the same temperature. Calculate the relative molecular mass of each gas and predict, with a reason, which diffuses faster. (Ar: Br = 80, N = 14, O = 16)
items.answer: Mr: Br₂ = 160, NO₂ = 46; nitrogen dioxide diffuses faster because its molecules are lighter and move faster at the same temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr values; 1 mark: nitrogen dioxide with reason [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, a student in Seoul, compares the rates of diffusion of helium, He, and methane, CH₄, at the same temperature. Calculate the relative molecular mass of each gas and predict, with a reason, which diffuses faster. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, He = 4)
items.answer: Mr: He = 4, CH₄ = 16; helium diffuses faster because its molecules are lighter and move faster at the same temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each Mr [2]; 1 mark: helium; 1 mark: lighter molecules move faster [1] total [4]

items.stem: In which state are the forces of attraction between the particles weakest?
options: they are equal in all three states
items.answer: gas
items.markingKey: Gas particles are far apart so attractive forces are negligible.

items.stem: Explain why a gas has a much lower density than the same substance as a liquid.
items.answer: In the gas the same mass of particles is spread over a much larger volume because the particles are far apart.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles far apart in gas; 1 mark: same mass occupies larger volume [2]

items.stem: Compare the arrangement and the movement of the particles in a liquid and in a gas.
items.answer: Liquid: particles close together, random arrangement, slide past each other. Gas: particles far apart, random arrangement, move rapidly in all directions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: liquid close/random; 1 mark: gas far apart; 1 mark: comparison of movement [3]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. magnesium: m.p. 650 °C, b.p. 1090 °C; ethanol: m.p. −114 °C, b.p. 78 °C; lead: m.p. 327 °C, b.p. 1749 °C; water: m.p. 0 °C, b.p. 100 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at −50 °C.
items.answer: magnesium: solid; ethanol: liquid; lead: solid; water: solid
items.markingKey: magnesium: solid; ethanol: liquid; lead: solid; water: solid. Solid if −50 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. iron: m.p. 1538 °C, b.p. 2862 °C; water: m.p. 0 °C, b.p. 100 °C; methane: m.p. −182 °C, b.p. −162 °C; nitrogen: m.p. −210 °C, b.p. −196 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at 25 °C.
items.answer: iron: solid; water: liquid; methane: gas; nitrogen: gas
items.markingKey: iron: solid; water: liquid; methane: gas; nitrogen: gas. Solid if 25 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: In a chemistry club, a sealed sample of argon (m.p. −189 °C, b.p. −186 °C) is studied at different temperatures. (a) Describe the arrangement and movement of the particles at −91 °C. (b) Explain, in terms of particles, why argon at −91 °C can be compressed.
items.answer: (a) far apart and randomly arranged; move rapidly and randomly in all directions (b) Particles are far apart with large spaces between them that can be reduced.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark arrangement; 1 mark movement [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which change of state releases energy to the surroundings?
items.answer: freezing
items.markingKey: Freezing and condensation are exothermic: attractive forces form.

items.stem: Explain why melting is described as an endothermic change.
items.answer: Energy must be taken in from the surroundings to overcome the forces of attraction holding the particles in the lattice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: energy taken in; 1 mark: to overcome forces between particles [2]

items.stem: Lucas heats a sample of naphthalene until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 100 °C, 1 min: 95 °C, 2 min: 90 °C, 3 min: 85 °C, 4 min: 80 °C, 5 min: 80 °C, 6 min: 80 °C, 7 min: 80 °C, 8 min: 74 °C, 9 min: 68 °C, 10 min: 62 °C. Use the results to state the freezing point of the sample and the physical state(s) present at 5 min.
items.answer: 80 °C; liquid and solid together
items.markingKey: 1 mark: freezing point; 1 mark: solid and liquid [2]

items.stem: Mateo heats a sample of octadecanoic acid until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 109 °C, 0.5 min: 103 °C, 1 min: 97 °C, 1.5 min: 91 °C, 2 min: 85 °C, 2.5 min: 79 °C, 3 min: 73 °C, 3.5 min: 69 °C, 4 min: 69 °C, 4.5 min: 69 °C, 5 min: 69 °C, 5.5 min: 69 °C, 6 min: 63 °C, 6.5 min: 57 °C, 7 min: 51 °C, 7.5 min: 45 °C. (a) State the physical state(s) present at 0 min and at 4 min. (b) Calculate how long the substance took to freeze completely, according to these readings.
items.answer: (a) liquid; liquid and solid (b) about 2 min

items.stem: In a college laboratory, a heating curve is plotted for aluminium (m.p. 660 °C, b.p. 2519 °C) from 620 °C to 2539 °C. (a) Describe the changes in the arrangement and movement of particles as the aluminium melts. (b) A second student finds that their sample melts between 654 °C and 658 °C. Suggest what this shows about their sample. (c) State whether boiling is endothermic or exothermic and give a reason.
items.answer: (a) Particles go from a regular arrangement vibrating about fixed points to a random arrangement sliding past one another. (b) It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range. (c) Endothermic: energy is taken in to overcome the attractive forces.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark arrangement; 1 mark movement [2] (b) 1 mark: impure; 1 mark: lower / over a range [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: The plunger of a sealed syringe of air is pushed in. What happens to the volume of the gas inside?
items.answer: It decreases.
items.markingKey: The pressure on the gas increases, so the volume decreases.

items.stem: Explain why a gas can be compressed much more than a liquid when pressure is applied.
items.answer: There are large spaces between gas particles that can be reduced; liquid particles are already touching.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Priya traps carbon dioxide in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 0 °C: 50.0 cm³, 25 °C: 54.6 cm³, 50 °C: ? cm³, 75 °C: 63.7 cm³, 100 °C: 68.3 cm³. (a) Estimate the missing volume. (b) Predict the volume at 125 °C.
items.answer: (a) 59.2 cm³ (accept ±0.2) (b) 72.9 cm³
items.markingKey: (a) mid-way between neighbouring readings [1] (b) continues the same increase of 4.6 cm³ per 25 °C [1]

items.stem: Sipho traps helium in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 10 °C: 60.0 cm³, 20 °C: 62.1 cm³, 30 °C: ? cm³, 40 °C: 66.4 cm³, 50 °C: 68.5 cm³. (a) Explain the trend in terms of particles. (b) Suggest why the syringe plunger must move freely.
items.answer: (a) Higher temperature → particles move faster → hit the plunger harder and more often → plunger pushed out until pressure balanced. (b) So that the pressure inside stays equal to atmospheric pressure (constant pressure).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: faster particles; 1 mark: more / harder collisions push plunger out [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: A company in Bangkok stores methane in cylinders and balloons for use at events. Engineers study how the gas behaves when it is heated, cooled and compressed. (a) Describe and explain what happens to the volume of the gas when it is heated at constant pressure. (b) Describe and explain what happens to the volume when the pressure is increased at constant temperature. (c) Suggest why gases are stored under high pressure in cylinders.
items.answer: (a) Volume increases: particles gain kinetic energy, move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, pushing them out. (b) Volume decreases: particles are far apart and are pushed closer together. (c) A large amount (mass) of gas can be stored in a small volume because the particles can be pushed close together.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: increases; 1 mark: faster particles; 1 mark: collisions with walls [3] (b) 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: particles pushed closer / spaces reduced [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: A student says, "Diffusion stops when the particles are evenly spread out." Explain whether this is correct.
items.answer: Particles keep moving randomly; there is no longer any net movement because the concentration is the same everywhere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles keep moving; 1 mark: no net movement [2]

items.stem: Explain why diffusion does not happen noticeably in solids.
items.answer: Particles in a solid only vibrate about fixed positions, so they cannot move past one another.

items.stem: Felix, a student in Colombo, compares the rates of diffusion of fluorine, F₂, and hydrogen bromide, HBr, at the same temperature. Calculate the relative molecular mass of each gas and predict, with a reason, which diffuses faster. (Ar: Br = 80, F = 19, H = 1)
items.answer: Mr: F₂ = 38, HBr = 81; fluorine diffuses faster because its molecules are lighter and move faster at the same temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr values; 1 mark: fluorine with reason [2]

items.stem: Aisha drops a crystal of ink into a beaker of still water at 30 °C and times how long it takes for the blue colour to spread evenly: 360 s. The experiment is repeated with water at 60 °C: 250 s. (a) Explain the difference between the two results. (b) State two variables that should be kept the same in both experiments.
items.answer: (a) At 60 °C the particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so diffusion is faster (250 s < 360 s). (b) size/mass of crystal; volume of water (also same beaker, no stirring)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: higher temperature faster; 1 mark: particles have more energy [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Why can a gas be compressed easily?
options: Its particles vibrate about fixed positions.
There are large spaces between its particles.
items.answer: There are large spaces between its particles.
items.markingKey: Gas particles are far apart, so they can be pushed closer together.

items.stem: Explain why the volume of a liquid stays the same when it is poured from a tall thin beaker into a wide dish.
items.answer: The particles stay close together held by attractive forces, so the volume is fixed; they can move past one another so the shape changes to fit the container.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: particles stay close / forces hold them; 1 mark: movement allows shape change [2]

items.stem: At −197 °C, octane (m.p. −57 °C, b.p. 126 °C) is in one physical state. Identify the state, describe the arrangement, movement and attractive forces of its particles, and use these to explain one property of octane at this temperature.
items.answer: Solid: particles closely packed in a regular arrangement (lattice); they vibrate about fixed positions; attractive forces are strong. Property: fixed shape and fixed volume; cannot be compressed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: state; 1 mark: arrangement; 1 mark: movement; 1 mark: property linked to particles [4]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. ethanol: m.p. −114 °C, b.p. 78 °C; nitrogen: m.p. −210 °C, b.p. −196 °C; copper: m.p. 1085 °C, b.p. 2562 °C; hexane: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 69 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at −20 °C.
items.answer: ethanol: liquid; nitrogen: gas; copper: solid; hexane: liquid
items.markingKey: ethanol: liquid; nitrogen: gas; copper: solid; hexane: liquid. Solid if −20 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: Data for 4 substances are shown. bromine: m.p. −7 °C, b.p. 59 °C; hexane: m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 69 °C; sulfur: m.p. 115 °C, b.p. 445 °C; zinc: m.p. 420 °C, b.p. 907 °C. Deduce the physical state of each substance at 25 °C.
items.answer: bromine: liquid; hexane: liquid; sulfur: solid; zinc: solid
items.markingKey: bromine: liquid; hexane: liquid; sulfur: solid; zinc: solid. Solid if 25 °C < m.p.; liquid if between m.p. and b.p.; gas if > b.p. 1 mark per correct state [4]

items.stem: A data book in Bangkok gives the melting point of sodium as 98 °C and its boiling point as 883 °C. (a) Describe the arrangement and movement of the particles at 928 °C. (b) Explain, in terms of particles, why sodium at 928 °C can be compressed.
items.answer: (a) far apart and randomly arranged; move rapidly and randomly in all directions (b) Particles are far apart with large spaces between them that can be reduced.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark arrangement; 1 mark movement [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: On a cooling curve, why does the temperature stay constant while a liquid freezes?
options: Energy is taken in to break forces.
Energy is released as the forces of attraction between particles form.
items.answer: Energy is released as the forces of attraction between particles form.
items.markingKey: Energy given out balances heat loss, so temperature is constant at the freezing point.

items.stem: Explain how a cooling curve can show that a substance is pure.
items.answer: A pure substance freezes at a single fixed temperature, so the curve has a flat (horizontal) section; an impure substance freezes over a range so the curve slopes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: flat section at one temperature; 1 mark: impure freezes over a range [2]

items.stem: Ana heats a sample of salol (phenyl salicylate) until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 77 °C, 0.5 min: 71 °C, 1 min: 65 °C, 1.5 min: 59 °C, 2 min: 53 °C, 2.5 min: 47 °C, 3 min: 42 °C, 3.5 min: 42 °C, 4 min: 42 °C, 4.5 min: 42 °C, 5 min: 37 °C, 5.5 min: 32 °C, 6 min: 27 °C. Use the results to state the freezing point of the sample and the physical state(s) present at 3.5 min.
items.answer: 42 °C; liquid and solid together
items.markingKey: 1 mark: freezing point; 1 mark: solid and liquid [2]

items.stem: A sample of propanone is heated steadily from −125 °C to 86 °C and a heating curve is plotted. Which state(s) are present during the second flat section of the curve? Give the temperature of the first flat section and explain why the temperature is constant there.
items.answer: liquid and gas; flat sections at −95 °C (melting) and 56 °C (boiling); energy supplied overcomes attractive forces instead of raising kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: state(s); 1 mark: correct temperature; 1 mark: energy used to overcome forces [3]

items.stem: Arjun heats a solid sample of hexane at a steady rate from −135 °C until it has all turned to gas at 89 °C. (a) Describe the shape of the heating curve, naming the processes at each flat section. (b) Explain why hexane can evaporate at temperatures below 69 °C but cannot boil.
items.answer: (a) rises (solid warms), flat at −95 °C (melting), rises (liquid warms), flat at 69 °C (boiling), rises (gas warms) (b) Some surface particles have enough energy to escape at any temperature; boiling needs the vapour to form throughout the liquid, which only happens at the boiling point.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: two flat sections; 1 mark: temperatures; 1 mark: named melting and boiling [3] (b) 1 mark: surface particles with enough energy escape; 1 mark: boiling throughout at b.p. [2]

items.stem: A diver releases a bubble of air deep under the sea and it rises to the surface. What happens to the volume of the gas inside?
items.answer: It increases.
items.markingKey: The pressure on the gas decreases, so the volume increases.

items.stem: A weather balloon rises to a height where the air pressure is much lower. Explain, in terms of particles, what happens to the volume of the gas.
items.answer: The volume increases: the external pressure decreases, so the particles are able to spread further apart; fewer collisions are needed to balance the lower pressure.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct prediction; 1 mark: particle speed / spacing; 1 mark: collisions with walls [3]

items.stem: Sipho traps nitrogen in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 0 °C: 30.0 cm³, 20 °C: 32.2 cm³, 40 °C: 34.4 cm³, 60 °C: ? cm³, 80 °C: 38.8 cm³. Describe the relationship between temperature and volume shown by the data.
items.answer: As the temperature increases the volume increases (by equal amounts for equal temperature rises).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume increases with temperature; 1 mark: steady / linear [2]

items.stem: A fixed mass of helium is kept at constant temperature while the pressure on it is changed. Results: 100 kPa: 100 cm³, 125 kPa: 80.0 cm³, 150 kPa: 66.7 cm³, 200 kPa: 50.0 cm³, 250 kPa: 40.0 cm³. Describe the relationship between pressure and volume shown, and predict the volume at 500 kPa.
items.answer: As pressure increases the volume decreases; doubling the pressure halves the volume (pressure × volume is constant). At 500 kPa the volume would be 20.0 cm³.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume decreases as pressure increases; 1 mark: inverse (doubling P halves V); 1 mark: prediction 20.0 cm³ [3]

items.stem: Noah investigates how the volume of carbon dioxide changes. A sample is sealed in a gas syringe and placed in water baths at different temperatures, and then the plunger is pushed in at constant temperature. (a) Describe and explain what happens to the volume of the gas when it is heated at constant pressure. (b) Describe and explain what happens to the volume when the pressure is increased at constant temperature. (c) Suggest why gases are stored under high pressure in cylinders.
items.answer: (a) Volume increases: particles gain kinetic energy, move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, pushing them out. (b) Volume decreases: particles are far apart and are pushed closer together. (c) A large amount (mass) of gas can be stored in a small volume because the particles can be pushed close together.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: increases; 1 mark: faster particles; 1 mark: collisions with walls [3] (b) 1 mark: decreases; 1 mark: particles pushed closer / spaces reduced [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student says, "Diffusion stops when the particles are evenly spread out." Explain whether this is correct. (b) Explain why ammonia diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride.
items.answer: (a) Particles keep moving randomly; there is no longer any net movement because the concentration is the same everywhere. (b) Ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17) than hydrogen chloride (36.5), so at the same temperature its molecules move faster.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: particles keep moving; 1 mark: no net movement [2] (b) 1 mark: Mr comparison; 1 mark: lighter molecules move faster [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why ammonia diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride. (b) Explain why a coloured dye spreads more quickly through hot water than through cold water.
items.answer: (a) Ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17) than hydrogen chloride (36.5), so at the same temperature its molecules move faster. (b) In hot water the particles have more kinetic energy and move faster, so they spread out more quickly.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Mr comparison; 1 mark: lighter molecules move faster [2] (b) 1 mark: more kinetic energy; 1 mark: faster movement / faster diffusion [2]

items.stem: Zara places cotton wool soaked in concentrated aqueous ammonia at one end of a 100 cm glass tube and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other end, then seals both ends. After a few minutes a white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube. Calculate the relative molecular masses of ammonia and hydrogen chloride.
items.answer: NH₃ = 17; HCl = 36.5
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Freya drops a crystal of ink into a beaker of still water at 10 °C and times how long it takes for the blue colour to spread evenly: 360 s. The experiment is repeated with water at 20 °C: 300 s. (a) State two variables that should be kept the same in both experiments. (b) Predict, with a reason, whether ammonia gas would diffuse through air faster or slower than the coloured particles diffuse through water.
items.answer: (a) size/mass of crystal; volume of water (also same beaker, no stirring) (b) Faster: gas particles move faster and are further apart, so collide less often with other particles.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: faster; 1 mark: reason [2]
